body.text:
Osmanthus latte: home made osmanthus sauce, with a little sea salt milk cap.
Chestnut basque: the outside is baked a bit burnt, inside still soft.
Hot red wine (no alcohol version): cinnamon, orange skin and clove, suitable for rainy day.

why.label: foam
why.note: Cafés call this topping foam, not cap or cream. 'Milk cap' suggests a mushroom to readers. A learner might write 'milk cap' or 'milk top', which neither matches the drink.

why.label: sprinkled
why.note: The source's 撒 means the salt is scattered lightly over the top, not poured or stirred in. 'Sprinkled' keeps that light, scattered sense that 'with ... on top' alone loses.

why.label: on top
why.note: Keep the position in the same phrase as the verb so it reads as one topping, not a separate clause. The sentence already says 'with a little sea salt', so 'on top' completes the picture.

why.label: caramelised
why.note: 焦香 is a pleasant browned flavour. "Burnt" reads as a baking fault, which is what the reader in this thread reacts to. "Caramelised" names the good browning and suits a menu.

why.label: still
why.note: 依然 means the inside stays soft even though the outside has browned. Without "still", the softness reads as a separate fact rather than something that survives the browning.

why.label: caramelised outside, still soft inside
why.note: Menu lines are short noun phrases. "The outside is baked" reads like a cooking instruction, so drop "is" and "baked" and keep the product-description form.

why.label: Mulled wine
why.note: Readers who see 'hot red wine' picture plain warm wine and expect alcohol. 'Mulled wine' is the standard English name for heated, spiced wine, so readers recognise the drink at once, and the '(alcohol-free)' note that follows then makes sense. 'Hot red wine' keeps the literal feel of the Chinese name.

note.meaning: Scattered lightly over the surface of something.
note.usage: Used for a light layer of salt, sugar, powder or herbs on food or drink. Better than 'with ... on top' because 'sprinkled' keeps the sense of light scattering.

examples.t: Sprinkled on top, the cocoa powder looked like a light dusting of snow.
examples.n: Scattered lightly over the surface, the cocoa powder looked like a light dusting of snow.

examples.t: Mum always sprinkled cinnamon on top of her apple cake before it went in the oven.
examples.n: Mum always scattered a little cinnamon over the top of her apple cake before baking it.

examples.t: A thin layer of snow sprinkled on top of the hills this morning.
examples.n: Overnight, a light covering of snow fell over the tops of the hills.

note.meaning: Browned or crisp on the outside, yet soft inside even after cooking.
note.usage: A standard menu formula for describing the texture of baked goods. 'Still' shows the softness survives the browning, which a plain 'soft inside' does not.

examples.t: Toasted outside, still tender inside, the lamb chops are our most ordered dish.
examples.n: Browned outside and still soft within, the lamb chops are our most ordered dish.

examples.t: The bread is toasted outside, still tender inside, so it works well with soup.
examples.n: The bread is crisp on the outside but soft inside, so it goes well with soup.

examples.t: Our scones are toasted outside, still tender inside, and best eaten warm.
examples.n: Our scones are golden on the outside, soft inside, and best eaten warm.

note.meaning: Wine heated and flavoured with spices, served hot.
note.usage: The standard English name for this drink on menus and in shops. Unlike 'hot red wine', it is recognised at once and signals that it is spiced, so readers do not expect alcohol unless told.

examples.t: We ordered two mulled wines and sat by the fire.
examples.n: We ordered two hot spiced wines and sat by the fire.

examples.t: Every December the market stall sells mulled wine in paper cups.
examples.n: Each December the market stall sells hot spiced wine in paper cups.

examples.t: My grandmother's mulled wine recipe uses orange slices and star anise.
examples.n: My grandmother's hot spiced wine recipe uses orange slices and star anise.

note.meaning: Made by the café or restaurant itself, not bought in.
note.usage: Used on menus for sauces, syrups, breads and other items the kitchen prepares. It is the menu term where 'home made' sounds literal and too domestic.

examples.t: The house-made osmanthus sauce is sweet but not heavy.
examples.n: The sauce that the café makes itself, with osmanthus, is sweet but not heavy.

examples.t: Every pastry on the counter is house-made, so the bakery sells out by noon.
examples.n: The bakery makes all its own pastries, so they sell out by noon.

examples.t: Ask for the house-made lemonade if you want something less sweet than the bottled kind.
examples.n: Ask for the lemonade the shop makes itself if you want something less sweet than the bottled kind.
